paragraphs.context: “Did Mama sing every day?” asked Caleb. “Every-single
paragraphs.simple: Caleb sits by the fire in the evening and asks his sister Anna if their mother sang every day.

background.note: Flat stones in front of a fireplace. Families on the prairie long ago warmed their homes with wood fires.

paragraphs.context: “Every-single-day,” I told him for the second
paragraphs.simple: Anna says yes. Caleb asks this question again and again, many times every week and every year.

paragraphs.context: “Yes. Papa sang, too. Don’t get so close, Caleb
paragraphs.simple: Anna says Papa also sang. She tells Caleb not to sit so close to the fire, or he will get too hot.

paragraphs.context: He pushed his chair back. It made a hollow
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dogs wake up a little.
paragraphs.simple: Caleb pushes his chair back with a loud sound. The dogs move. Lottie lifts her head, but Nick keeps sleeping.

paragraphs.context: I turned the bread dough over and over on
paragraphs.simple: Anna is making bread. She turns the soft dough again and again on a stone table top.

paragraphs.context: “Well, Papa doesn’t sing anymore,” said Caleb very softly
paragraphs.simple: Caleb says softly that Papa does not sing any more. A burning log breaks in the fire. Then Caleb asks what he looked like as a new baby.

paragraphs.context: “You didn’t have any clothes on,” I told him.
paragraphs.simple: Anna jokes that the new baby Caleb had no clothes on.

paragraphs.context: “You looked like this.” I held the bread dough
paragraphs.simple: Anna holds up the round, pale ball of bread dough and says Caleb looked like that.

paragraphs.context: “I had hair,” said Caleb seriously.
paragraphs.simple: Caleb says, very seriously, that he had hair. Anna says there was very little hair.

paragraphs.context: “And she named me Caleb,” he went on, filling
paragraphs.simple: Caleb goes on telling the old story that he knows so well: Mama named him Caleb.

paragraphs.context: “I would have named you Troublesome,” I said, making
paragraphs.simple: Anna says she would have named him 'Troublesome', a name for a child who makes trouble. Caleb smiles.

paragraphs.context: “And Mama handed me to you in the yellow
paragraphs.simple: Caleb says Mama gave him to Anna in a yellow blanket, and waits for Anna to say Mama's words.

paragraphs.context: I sighed. “And Mama said, ‘Isn’t he beautiful, Anna?’”
paragraphs.simple: Anna sighs and says Mama's words: 'Isn't he beautiful, Anna?'

paragraphs.context: “And I was,” Caleb finished.
paragraphs.simple: Caleb says the last line himself: he was beautiful.

paragraphs.context: Caleb thought the story was over, and I didn’t
paragraphs.simple: Anna did not think baby Caleb was beautiful. He was not pretty, he cried loudly and smelled bad. But the worst thing was that Mama died the next morning.

paragraphs.context: “Isn’t he beautiful, Anna?” Her last words to me
paragraphs.simple: Mama's question was the last thing she said to Anna. Anna went to bed thinking Caleb looked terrible, and she forgot to say good night to Mama.

paragraphs.context: I wiped my hands on my apron and went
paragraphs.simple: Anna looks out of the window at the wide, flat land and the long road. She remembers the sunny morning Mama died, and the family who came but could not fill the empty house.

background.note: The wide grassland in the middle of the USA. In the late 1800s, many farm families lived there, far from towns and from each other.

paragraphs.context: Slowly, one by one, they left. And then the
paragraphs.simple: One by one the relatives went home. Every day felt long and dark, and Papa stopped singing.

paragraphs.context: Isn’t he beautiful, Anna?
paragraphs.simple: Anna remembers Mama's words: 'Isn't he beautiful, Anna?'

paragraphs.context: It was hard to think of Caleb as beautiful
paragraphs.simple: It took Anna three days to love her baby brother. She sat by the fire with him, and his tiny hand touched her face. It was his smile that won her heart.

paragraphs.context: “Can you remember her songs?” asked Caleb. “Mama’s songs?”
paragraphs.simple: Caleb asks if Anna can remember Mama's songs.

paragraphs.context: I turned from the window. “No. Only that she
paragraphs.simple: Anna cannot remember the songs. She only remembers that Mama sang about flowers, birds and the moon.

paragraphs.context: Caleb reached down and touched Lottie’s head.
paragraphs.simple: Caleb reaches down and touches Lottie's head.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe,” he said, his voice low, “if you remember
paragraphs.simple: Caleb says quietly that if Anna remembers the songs, maybe he can remember Mama too.

paragraphs.context: My eyes widened and tears came. Then the door
paragraphs.simple: Anna's eyes fill with tears. Then Papa comes in with the cold wind. He hugs Anna and smells her hair.

paragraphs.simple: Papa says the stew smells nice and soapy.

paragraphs.simple: Papa says he has forgotten the old songs. But he thinks there may be a way to remember them.

paragraphs.simple: The letter is from Sarah Wheaton of Maine. She has never married. She lives with her brother William, who is going to marry a young woman.

paragraphs.simple: Sarah loves the sea, but she feels she must move now. She is strong and works hard, but she is not always quiet and gentle. She wants to know about the children and Papa.

paragraphs.simple: At the end of the letter Sarah asks if they like cats, because she has one.

paragraphs.simple: Anna breaks the quiet. She has one more thing to say.

paragraphs.simple: Anna asks Papa to write and ask Sarah if she sings. Singing is what the family has lost.

paragraphs.simple: Sarah can braid hair, make stew and bake bread. But she likes building bookshelves and painting more.

paragraphs.simple: Sarah loves the colors of the sea: blue, gray and green. Her brother is a fisherman. She sends a book of sea birds so Anna can see what she sees every day.

paragraphs.context: Caleb read and read the letter so many times
paragraphs.simple: Caleb reads the letter so many times that the ink spreads and the paper tears. He reads the bird book again and again.

paragraphs.simple: Caleb wonders if Sarah will come and stay. He is afraid she will think they are noisy and annoying.

paragraphs.simple: Anna says Caleb is noisy and annoying. But she is worried too. Sarah loves the sea, and their home has only fields and sky.

paragraphs.simple: Caleb worries that Sarah will not like their small house. He is sorry he told her it was small.

paragraphs.simple: Sarah's cat is called Seal because she is gray like the seals in the sea. Sarah jokes that Seal sends her own footprint back to the dogs.

paragraphs.simple: Sarah likes small rooms sometimes and can keep a fire burning at night. She does not know if she snores, because her cat has never told her.

paragraphs.simple: Anna cannot believe Caleb asked Sarah about fires and snoring.

paragraphs.context: “I wished to know,” Caleb said.
paragraphs.simple: Caleb says he wanted to know.

paragraphs.context: He kept the letter with him, reading it in
paragraphs.simple: Caleb carries the letter with him everywhere and reads it all day, even in bed.

paragraphs.simple: One early morning the family is cleaning the horse stalls. Papa suddenly stops and leans on his tool.

paragraphs.simple: Papa says Sarah will come for one month, to see how she likes it.

paragraphs.simple: Caleb stands by the stall door with his arms crossed, thinking.

paragraphs.simple: Caleb says slowly that he thinks it would be good to say yes. Then he says it very fast.

paragraphs.simple: Papa says yes. They will invite Sarah.

paragraphs.simple: All three of them smile and go back to work.

paragraphs.simple: Papa says the cat will be useful in the barn to catch mice.

paragraphs.simple: They see a huge black cloud coming over the fields. Papa slides down the roof and helps Sarah down.

paragraphs.simple: Papa shouts that a sudden storm is coming. He holds up his arms, and Sarah jumps down from the porch roof.

paragraphs.simple: Papa tells the children to bring the horses, sheep and cows inside. The barn is the safest place.

paragraphs.simple: The grass is pushed flat, the light turns yellow, and the rain gets louder. The children bring the animals in. Sarah and Papa come with food and the dogs.

paragraphs.simple: Sarah cries out that her chickens are still outside.

paragraphs.simple: Sarah runs into the heavy rain, and Papa follows. The animals are scared. Then Sarah and Papa come back, very wet, with the chickens and an armful of roses.

paragraphs.simple: The chickens sit calmly in the hay. Papa closes the door. In the dim barn he puts blankets on them, and Sarah unpacks food and her shells.

paragraphs.simple: Caleb goes to the small barn window.

paragraphs.simple: Caleb asks what color the sea is in a storm.

paragraphs.context: “Blue,” said Sarah, brushing her wet hair back with
paragraphs.simple: Sarah says it is blue, gray and green.

paragraphs.simple: Caleb tells Sarah to look: the storm colors show what is missing from her drawing.

paragraphs.context: Sarah went to stand between Caleb and Papa by
paragraphs.simple: Sarah stands by the window between Caleb and Papa and looks for a long time. Then she touches Papa's shoulder.

paragraphs.simple: Sarah says they have storms like this in Maine too. She tells Papa it will be all right.

paragraphs.context: Papa said nothing. But he put his arm around
paragraphs.simple: Papa puts his arm around Sarah. Anna remembers Mama and Papa standing like that. When she opens her eyes, it is Sarah. Caleb smiles and smiles.

paragraphs.simple: They sleep in the barn. At dawn hail falls like stones. When it stops, the ground is white and shining, like the sea.

paragraphs.simple: It is very quiet. The dogs eat the hail. A tree has fallen near the pond, and roses lie on the ground, as if after a wedding. Sarah is only glad she saved some.

paragraphs.simple: Only one field is badly hurt. Sarah and Papa plow and plant it again. The roof did not break.

paragraphs.context: “I told you I know about roofs,” Sarah told
paragraphs.simple: Sarah reminds Papa that she knows about roofs, and he smiles.

paragraphs.context: Papa kept his promise to Sarah. When the work
paragraphs.simple: Papa keeps his promise. He teaches Sarah to ride. She rides Old Bess and learns very quickly.

paragraphs.context: “Too quick,” Caleb complained to me as we watched
paragraphs.simple: Caleb says she learns too fast. He hopes she will fall and have to stay. He asks Anna why Sarah has to go alone.

paragraphs.context: “Hush up, Caleb,” I said crossly. “Hush up.”
paragraphs.simple: Anna angrily tells Caleb to be quiet. She is worried too.

paragraphs.context: “I could get sick and make her stay here

paragraphs.context: “We could tie her up.”
paragraphs.simple: Caleb says they could tie her up.

paragraphs.context: And Caleb began to cry, and I took him
paragraphs.simple: Caleb starts to cry. Anna takes him into the barn, and they both cry.

paragraphs.context: Papa and Sarah came to hitch the horses to
paragraphs.simple: Papa teaches Sarah to drive the wagon. He sends Caleb to cut up the fallen tree. Anna watches, then goes into the dark barn.

paragraphs.context: “Why?” I asked out loud, echoing Caleb’s question.
paragraphs.simple: Anna asks 'Why?' out loud, the same question Caleb asked.

paragraphs.context: The chickens watched me, their eyes small and bright.
paragraphs.simple: The chickens look at Anna with small, bright eyes.

paragraphs.context: The next morning Sarah got up early and put
paragraphs.simple: The next morning Sarah puts on her blue dress, gives the horses apples and hay, and puts on her yellow bonnet.

paragraphs.context: “Remember Jack,” said Papa. “A strong hand.”
paragraphs.simple: Papa reminds her to hold Jack's reins firmly.

paragraphs.context: “Best to be home before dark,” said Papa. “Driving
paragraphs.simple: Papa says she should come home before dark, because driving is hard without moonlight.

paragraphs.context: Sarah kissed us all, even my father, who looked
paragraphs.simple: Sarah kisses them all, even Papa, who is surprised.

paragraphs.context: “Take care of Seal,” she said to Caleb and
paragraphs.simple: Sarah asks the children to take care of Seal. She speaks gently to Old Bess and firmly to Jack, and drives away alone.

paragraphs.context: “Very good,” murmured Papa as he watched. And after
paragraphs.simple: Papa says quietly that she drives well. After a while he goes to the fields.

paragraphs.context: Caleb and I watched Sarah from the porch. Caleb
paragraphs.simple: Anna and Caleb watch from the porch. Anna remembers another sunny day when a wagon took Mama away, and Mama never came back.

paragraphs.context: Seal jumped up to the porch, her feet making
paragraphs.simple: Anna sweeps the porch and waters Sarah's plants. Caleb spills ashes, so Anna must sweep again.

paragraphs.context: “I am loud and pesky,” Caleb cried sud-denly
paragraphs.simple: Caleb cries that he is noisy and annoying, and that Sarah has gone to buy a train ticket to leave.

paragraphs.context: “No, Caleb. She would tell us.”
paragraphs.simple: Anna says Sarah would tell them if she was leaving.

paragraphs.simple: Caleb thinks the house is too small for Sarah.

paragraphs.simple: Anna says the house is not too small.

paragraphs.context: I looked at Sarah’s drawing of the fields pinned
paragraphs.simple: Anna looks at Sarah's drawing of the fields on the wall.

paragraphs.context: “What is missing?” I asked Caleb. “You said you
paragraphs.simple: Anna asks Caleb what he thinks is missing from the drawing.

paragraphs.context: “Colors,” said Caleb wearily. “The colors of the sea.”
paragraphs.simple: Caleb says, tired and sad, that the colors of the sea are missing.

paragraphs.context: Outside, clouds moved into the sky and went away
paragraphs.simple: Clouds come and go. The children take lunch to Papa. Caleb pushes Anna to ask him something.

paragraphs.context: “Ask him. Ask Papa.”
paragraphs.simple: Caleb wants Anna to ask Papa.

paragraphs.context: “What has Sarah gone to do?” I asked.
paragraphs.simple: Anna asks Papa what Sarah has gone to do.

paragraphs.context: “I don’t know,” said Papa. He squinted at me
paragraphs.simple: Papa does not know. He sighs and touches both children's heads. He says Sarah does things her own way.

paragraphs.context: “I know,” said Caleb very softly.
paragraphs.simple: Caleb says very softly that he knows.

paragraphs.context: Papa picked up his shovel and put on his
paragraphs.simple: Papa picks up his shovel and puts on his hat.

paragraphs.context: “Ask if she’s coming back,” whispered Caleb.
paragraphs.simple: Caleb whispers to Anna to ask if Sarah is coming back.

paragraphs.context: “Of course she’s coming back,” I said. “Seal is
paragraphs.simple: Anna says of course Sarah is coming back, because her cat is still here. But she does not ask Papa; she is afraid of the answer.

paragraphs.context: We fed the sheep, and I set the table
paragraphs.simple: Anna sets the table for four. The sun goes down, Papa lights the stove, and it gets dark. Caleb sits on the steps, turning his shell.

paragraphs.simple: Suddenly Lottie barks and Nick runs down the road.

paragraphs.context: “Dust!” cried Caleb. He climbed the porch and stood

paragraphs.context: Slowly the wagon came around the windmill and the
paragraphs.simple: The wagon slowly comes around the windmill and the barn into the yard, with the dogs jumping happily.

paragraphs.context: “Hush, dogs,” said Sarah. And Nick leaped up into
paragraphs.simple: Sarah tells the dogs to be quiet, and Nick jumps into the wagon next to her.

paragraphs.context: Papa took the reins and Sarah climbed down from
paragraphs.simple: Papa takes the reins, and Sarah climbs down.

paragraphs.context: Caleb burst into tears.
paragraphs.simple: Caleb suddenly starts to cry.

paragraphs.context: “Seal was very worried!” he cried.
paragraphs.simple: Caleb cries that Seal was very worried. He really means he was worried.

paragraphs.context: Sarah put her arms around him, and he wailed
paragraphs.simple: Sarah hugs him, and he cries into her dress. He says they thought the house was too small and he was too noisy.

paragraphs.context: Sarah looked at Papa and me over Caleb’s head.
paragraphs.simple: Sarah looks at Papa and Anna over Caleb's head.

paragraphs.context: “We thought you might be thinking of leaving us
paragraphs.simple: Anna tells Sarah they thought she might leave because she misses the sea.

paragraphs.context: “No,” she said. “I will always miss my old
paragraphs.simple: Sarah says she will always miss her old home, but she would miss them more. She is staying.

paragraphs.context: Papa smiled at Sarah, then he bent quickly to
paragraphs.simple: Papa smiles at Sarah, then quickly takes the horses to the barn to drink.

paragraphs.context: Sarah handed me a package.
paragraphs.simple: Sarah gives Anna a package.

paragraphs.simple: Sarah says the gift is for Anna, Caleb and everyone.

paragraphs.context: The package was small, wrapped in brown paper with
paragraphs.simple: Anna carefully opens the small package. Inside are three colored pencils.

paragraphs.context: “Blue,” said Caleb slowly, “and gray. And green.”
paragraphs.simple: Caleb names the colors slowly: blue, gray and green, the colors of the sea.

paragraphs.context: “Papa,” he called. “Papa, come quickly! Sarah has brought
paragraphs.simple: Caleb calls Papa to come quickly. Sarah has brought the sea: the colors to finish her drawing.

paragraphs.context: We eat our night meal by candlelight, the four
paragraphs.simple: Now the family eats by candlelight. Sarah has brought candles, seeds and a song book. Soon there will be a wedding, and Papa will say 'Ayuh'.

background.note: A church minister who leads a wedding and asks the man and woman if they want to marry.

paragraphs.context: Autumn will come, then winter, cold with a wind
paragraphs.simple: Anna thinks of the seasons to come: winter wind, nests of curls, dried flowers, the rope in storms, Sarah's sea on the wall, songs, and Sarah, plain and tall.

sentences.context: And the truth is, the sea is as far east as I can go.
sentences.simple: To tell the truth, I cannot move any further east, because the sea is there.

parts.text: And the truth is,
parts.meaning: Honestly,

parts.text: the sea is as far east as I can go.
parts.meaning: I cannot go further east than the sea.

sentences.grammar: "As far east as I can go" = the most eastern place I can go. So if Sarah moves, she must go west.

sentences.context: But these were not the worst of him.
sentences.simple: But these things were not the worst thing about him.

parts.text: But these were not the worst of him.
parts.meaning: But these were not the worst things about him.

sentences.grammar: "These" points back to his looks, his cry and his smell. "The worst of him" = the worst thing about him.

sentences.context: He was homely and plain, and he had a terrible holler and a horrid smell.
sentences.simple: Baby Caleb was not pretty, he cried very loudly and he smelled bad.
sentences.main: Anna did not think Caleb was beautiful.

parts.text: He was homely and plain,
parts.meaning: He was not nice to look at,

parts.text: and he had a terrible holler and a horrid smell.
parts.meaning: and he cried loudly and smelled bad.

sentences.grammar: "Homely" and "plain" both mean "not pretty" here. "Holler" = a loud cry.

sentences.context: If you should still care to write, I would be interested in your children and about where you live.

parts.text: If you should still care to write,
parts.meaning: If you still want to write,

parts.text: I would be interested in your children and about where you live.
parts.meaning: I would like to know about your children and your home.

sentences.grammar: "If you should..." is a polite, old-fashioned way to say "if you...". "Care to" = want to.

sentences.context: My choice, as you can see, is limited.
sentences.simple: As you can understand, I do not have many choices.

parts.text: My choice,
parts.meaning: My choice

parts.text: as you can see,
parts.meaning: as you understand,

parts.text: is limited.
parts.meaning: is small.

sentences.grammar: The words "as you can see" are added in the middle. "Limited" means small, not many.

sentences.context: Not because he meant to, but because he had been thinking of it for so long.
sentences.simple: He did not want to be rude; he spoke roughly because he had thought about it for a very long time.

parts.text: Not because he meant to,
parts.meaning: He did not plan to be rough,

parts.text: but because he had been thinking of it for so long.
parts.meaning: but he had thought about it for a long time.

sentences.grammar: "Not because A, but because B" = the reason is B, not A. "Had been thinking" = he was thinking for a long time before that moment.

sentences.context: Outside, the prairie reached out and touched the places where the sky came down.
sentences.simple: Outside, the flat land went on so far that it seemed to touch the sky.

parts.text: Outside,
parts.meaning: Out of the window,

parts.text: the prairie reached out and touched the places
parts.meaning: the land went very far and seemed to touch

parts.text: where the sky came down.
parts.meaning: where the sky seems to meet the land.

sentences.grammar: The writer talks about the land as if it were a person with arms ("reached out and touched"). This makes a picture in your mind.

sentences.context: Papa might not have told us about Sarah that night if Caleb hadn’t asked him the question.
sentences.simple: If Caleb had not asked the question, maybe Papa would not have told them about Sarah that night.

parts.text: Papa might not have told us about Sarah that night
parts.meaning: Maybe Papa would not have talked about Sarah

parts.text: if Caleb hadn’t asked him the question.
parts.meaning: if Caleb had not asked.

sentences.grammar: "Might not have told ... if ... hadn't asked" talks about the past that did not happen: Caleb did ask, so Papa did tell.

sentences.context: I think,” he said slowly, “that it would be good—to say yes,” he finished in a rush.
sentences.simple: Caleb said slowly that he thought it would be good to say yes. He said the last words very fast.

parts.meaning: Caleb said slowly that he thought

parts.text: “that it would be good—to say yes,”
parts.meaning: it would be good to say yes,

parts.text: he finished in a rush.
parts.meaning: he said the end very quickly.

sentences.grammar: The dash (—) shows that Caleb stops for a moment before the important words. "In a rush" = very fast.

sentences.context: Maybe she wouldn’t leave there after all to come where there were fields and grass and sky and not much else.
sentences.simple: Maybe in the end Sarah would not leave the sea to come to a place with only fields, grass and sky.
sentences.main: Anna is afraid Sarah won't come.

parts.text: Maybe she wouldn’t leave there after all
parts.meaning: Maybe in the end she would not leave her home

parts.text: to come where there were fields and grass and sky and not much else.
parts.meaning: to come to a place with only fields, grass and sky.

sentences.grammar: "After all" = in the end, after thinking about it. "Not much else" = almost nothing more.

sentences.context: I wished that Papa and Caleb and I were perfect for Sarah.
sentences.simple: Anna wanted her family to be just right for Sarah.

parts.text: I wished
parts.meaning: I wanted very much

parts.text: that Papa and Caleb and I were perfect for Sarah.
parts.meaning: that our family was just right for Sarah.

sentences.grammar: After "I wished", we use a past form ("were") for something that is not true now.

sentences.context: In a month’s time the preacher might come to marry Sarah and Papa.
sentences.simple: After one month, a minister might come to marry Sarah and Papa.

parts.text: In a month’s time
parts.meaning: One month from now,

parts.text: the preacher might come to marry Sarah and Papa.
parts.meaning: a minister might come for their wedding.

sentences.grammar: "In a month's time" = one month from now. "Might" shows it is possible but not sure.

sentences.context: The sea washes over and over and around the stone, rolling it until it is round and perfect.
sentences.simple: Sea water moves over the stone again and again and turns it, until the stone is round and perfect.
sentences.main: How the sea makes a perfect stone.

parts.meaning: The sea water moves over the stone many times,

parts.text: rolling it
parts.meaning: turning it over and over

parts.text: until it is round and perfect.
parts.meaning: until it becomes round and perfect.

sentences.grammar: "Over and over" = again and again. The -ing part ("rolling it") tells what the sea does at the same time.

sentences.context: Time enough for her to change her mind and leave us.
sentences.simple: That was enough time for Sarah to decide to go away.

parts.meaning: Enough time for Sarah

parts.text: to change her mind and leave us.
parts.meaning: to decide differently and go away.

sentences.grammar: This is not a full sentence; it adds an idea to the sentence before. "Time enough" = enough time. "Change her mind" = make a different choice.

sentences.context: It was called “Sumer Is Icumen in,” and she taught it to us all, even Papa, who sang as if he had never stopped singing.
sentences.simple: The song was 'Sumer Is Icumen in'. Sarah taught it to everyone, even Papa, and he sang as if he had always been singing.

parts.meaning: The song's name was 'Sumer Is Icumen in',

parts.text: and she taught it to us all, even Papa,
parts.meaning: and she taught everyone, even Papa,

parts.text: who sang as if he had never stopped singing.
parts.meaning: and Papa sang as if he had never stopped.

sentences.grammar: "Who" adds information about Papa. "As if" = in a way that makes it seem that... This is important: Papa sings again.

sentences.context: She put it to Caleb’s ear, then mine.
sentences.simple: She held the shell to Caleb's ear, and then she held it to Anna's ear.
sentences.grammar: "Then mine" means then to my ear. Anna does not say "to my ear" again.

sentences.context: Sliding down our dune of hay is almost as fine as sliding down the sand dunes into the sea.

parts.meaning: is nearly as good as

parts.text: sliding down the sand dunes into the sea.
parts.meaning: sliding down sand hills into the sea.

sentences.grammar: "Sliding down our dune" is the thing she is talking about. "Almost as ... as" means nearly the same. Sarah says "our dune": she feels part of the family.

sentences.context: The fields had turned to a sea that gleamed like sun on glass.
sentences.simple: In Anna's dream, the fields became a sea that shone brightly.

parts.meaning: The fields had become a sea

parts.text: that gleamed like sun on glass.
parts.meaning: that shone like the sun on a window.

sentences.grammar: "Turn to" = become. "That" begins a part that describes the sea.

sentences.context: There are always things to miss,” said Maggie. “No matter where you are.
sentences.simple: Maggie says that wherever you live, you will always miss something.

parts.meaning: You will always miss some things,

parts.meaning: Maggie said.

parts.text: “No matter where you are.
parts.meaning: It does not matter where you live.

sentences.grammar: "No matter where" = it is not important where; in every place.

sentences.context: I closed my eyes, suddenly remembering Mama and Papa standing that way, Mama smaller than Sarah, her hair fair against Papa’s shoulder.

parts.meaning: Anna closed her eyes,

parts.text: her hair fair against Papa’s shoulder.

sentences.grammar: "Remembering" tells what happens at the same time as she closes her eyes. The last two parts tell more about Mama.

sentences.context: And the wild roses were scattered on the ground, as if a wedding had come and gone there.

sentences.main: The roses look like wedding flowers.

parts.meaning: Roses lay all over the ground,

parts.text: as if a wedding had come and gone there.
parts.meaning: like after a wedding.

sentences.grammar: "As if" makes a picture: it looks like something happened. "Come and gone" = happened and ended.

sentences.context: Autumn will come, then winter, cold with a wind that blows like the wind off the sea in Maine.
sentences.simple: Autumn will come, and then a cold winter, with a wind like the sea wind in Maine.

parts.text: Autumn will come, then winter,
parts.meaning: Autumn and then winter will come,

parts.text: cold with a wind
parts.meaning: a cold winter with wind

parts.text: that blows like the wind off the sea in Maine.
parts.meaning: that is like the wind from the sea in Maine.

sentences.grammar: The story looks ahead to what will come. "Off the sea" means coming from the sea. The prairie now has something like Sarah's sea.

sentences.context: It was sunny, and I remembered another time when a wagon had taken Mama away.

parts.meaning: The day was sunny,

parts.text: and I remembered another time
parts.meaning: and Anna thought of another day

parts.text: when a wagon had taken Mama away.

a bit.example: Finally I turned my head a bit to sneak a look at Caleb.
a bit.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

a pair of.meaning: Two things that go together, or one thing with two parts, like pants.
a pair of.example: In the morning, Sarah dressed in a pair of overalls and went to the barn to have an argument with Papa.
a pair of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

about to.meaning: Going to happen or do something very soon.
about to.example: I have lived with an older brother, William, who is about to be married.
about to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

after a while.example: And after a while he turned and went out into the fields.
after a while.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

after all.meaning: In the end, even though you did not expect it.
after all.example: Maybe she wouldn’t leave there after all to come where there were fields and grass and sky and not much else.
after all.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

all right.example: It will be all right, Jacob.”
all right.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

all winter long.example: And we can have flowers all winter long.”
all winter long.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

any longer.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to know.

as far as.meaning: "As far as you can see" = to the farthest place you can see.
as far as.example: “It stretches out as far as you can see.
as far as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

as if.meaning: In a way that makes it seem that...
as if.example: It was called “Sumer Is Icumen in,” and she taught it to us all, even Papa, who sang as if he had never stopped singing.
as if.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

at first.meaning: At the start, before something changes.
at first.example: A few raindrops came, gentle at first, then stronger and louder, so that Caleb and I covered our ears and stared at each other without speaking.
at first.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

at last.example: At last Papa slid down, too, as the sky grew darker and the stars blinked like fireflies.
at last.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

at least.meaning: Used to say one thing is good, even when other things are bad.
at least.example: “At least Sarah can hear the sea,” he whispered.
at least.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

at the same time.example: “Summer,” said Papa and Sarah at the same time.
at the same time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

back and forth.meaning: First one way, then the other way, again and again.
back and forth.example: Caleb came over and threw his arms around Papa’s neck and hung down as Papa swung him back and forth, and the dogs sat up.
back and forth.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

because of.example: My house is tall and the shingles are gray because of the salt from the sea.
because of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

before dark.example: “Best to be home before dark,” said Papa.
before dark.usageNote: A very common phrase. Good to learn.

blue-eyed grass.meaning: A small wild plant with blue flowers and leaves like grass.
blue-eyed grass.example: She came through green grass fields that bloomed with Indian paintbrush, red and orange, and blue-eyed grass.
blue-eyed grass.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.

bride's bonnet.meaning: The name of a small wild flower (its shape looks a little like a hat).
bride's bonnet.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.

burst into tears.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

burst out laughing.example: Caleb and I looked at each other and burst out laughing, remembering Hilly, our old housekeeper.
burst out laughing.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

by yourself.meaning: Alone, with nobody else; without help.
by yourself.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

catch yourself.meaning: To suddenly notice what you are doing and stop. "Caught myself" = I noticed my mistake and stopped.
catch yourself.example: Once I set four places at the table, then caught myself and put the extra plate away.
catch yourself.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

change your mind.meaning: To make a different choice from before.
change your mind.example: Time enough for her to change her mind and leave us.
change your mind.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

close by.example: And then, as the thunder pounded and the wind rose and there was the terrible crackling of lightning close by, Sarah and Papa stood in the barn doorway, wet to the skin.
close by.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

conch shell.meaning: A big, pointed sea shell. If you hold it to your ear, you seem to hear the sea.
